headline: Splitting the same page across five modules costs next-yak's styled API its entire build-time fold and lands it on the lane that never folds, while the css prop resolves imported fragments at build time and holds its position.

microbench.why: The tile, the DOM, the CSS and the 400 products are byte-identical to the Example `product-grid`; only the file layout changes, which leaves folding as the variable. `next-yak` now declares its primitives in `layout.ts`, `controls.ts` and `text.ts` while the JSX using them lives in `index.tsx`, so `fold_jsx_usages` never sees a declaration and its use site in one module. Every primitive stays a runtime `Yak` wrapper and lib self-time rises from 0.616 ms to 1.689 ms, within 5% of the 1.610 ms `next-yak-nofold` pays with folding switched off. `next-yak-css` keeps 0.000 ms of lib time because the css prop folds on the element where it is written and inlines an imported fragment at build time. StyleX pays a smaller version of the same bill, its `props()` call going from 0.112 ms to 0.680 ms once `stylex.create` sits behind an import.

autocannon.why: Throughput falls from 236 req/s to 166 for `next-yak`, a 30% cut for a change that moved no CSS and no markup. `next-yak-css` holds at 264 req/s. The runtime lanes stay flat within noise, which is the control the case needs: they never had a build-time optimization to lose, so any movement there would mean the port leaked something.

attribution.why: `vanilla` and `next-yak-css` hold the 2.1 ms floor they set on the single-file page, so a module boundary costs nothing to anything that resolves at build time wherever the source lives. `next-yak` climbs to 4.15 ms from 2.42 ms and the entire increase is lib self-time, 1.689 ms against 0.616 ms. Both StyleX lanes gain about 0.6 ms in the same slice for the same reason.

hydrate.why: Hydration re-runs the render on the client and inherits the loss: `next-yak` needs 68.8 ms against 59.6 ms on the single-file page, while `next-yak-css` stays at 55.9 ms. The lanes that rebuild a sheet during hydration are unchanged at 234 ms and 247 ms, because their cost never depended on file layout.

inp.why: Interaction carries the largest relative cost of the split. The wishlist toggle takes 20.8 ms in `next-yak` against 9.4 ms on the single-file page, because the click now re-renders through runtime wrappers instead of swapping a class string the compiler already resolved. `next-yak-css` answers in 7.7 ms either way. This is the axis a user feels directly, and it more than doubles.

mount.why: Cold mount absorbs the split better than interaction does, since parse and layout are identical across lanes and dominate the measurement: `next-yak` moves from 129 ms to 141 ms. The rest of the ordering matches the single-file page, `next-yak-css` at 125 ms and the runtime lanes above 200 ms.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, identical to the single-file page, with the sub-millisecond costs inside the same 0.245 ms to 0.736 ms band. Splitting the source changes what runs during render, not what the engine has to match afterwards.

payload.why: The split is nearly free on the wire, which settles the obvious worry that fragments shared by three modules would be emitted three times. `next-yak` ships 932 gz B of CSS against 918 B on the single-file page and 8,425 B in total against 8,291 B, so `focusRing` and `minTargetSize` reach `controls.ts`, `text.ts` and `button.ts` and are written once. Every lane's JS is byte-identical to the single-file case, since file layout does not change what the library ships.

nsweep.why: At 4,000 tiles the split costs `next-yak` 40.8 ms against 21.3 ms on the single-file page, and it now tracks `next-yak-nofold` at 41.2 ms. Per-element wrapper work sets a slope rather than an offset, so the penalty grows with the size of the page.

crossCase: This is the Example `product-grid` shown above with nothing changed but the file layout: same DOM, same CSS, same 400 products, verified pixel-identical, which is what makes the module boundary the only variable. Read it against the Example `multifile-composition`, which moves the styled primitives and their JSX use sites together into one imported module and therefore keeps folding, at 87,000 renders/s against `tabs`'s 88,200. Moving a whole component across a file is free; shipping primitives for another module to use is not.
